clinicalPearls: Bow legs are normal in infants and toddlers, forming part of a physiological sequence that moves from varus in the first two years toward valgus by about three to four years before settling into the mild adult valgus
Physiological genu varum is symmetrical, painless, and associated with normal stature, and it improves steadily with growth
The intercondylar distance measured with the ankles together helps to quantify and monitor the degree of bowing over time
Blount disease (infantile tibia vara) is the most important pathological cause and produces a sharp, progressive metaphyseal angulation, often in early-walking, overweight children
The metaphyseal-diaphyseal (Drennan) angle on a standing radiograph helps distinguish physiological bowing from Blount disease
Rickets, whether nutritional or hypophosphataemic, is a key metabolic cause and is suggested by short stature, metaphyseal widening, and biochemical abnormalities
Management of physiological bowing is reassurance and observation, whereas pathological varus may need bracing, guided growth, or corrective osteotomy
reference.pathophysiology: Genu varum refers to an outward (varus) angulation at the knee so that the legs bow apart. Physiological bow legs reflect the normal alignment of the immature skeleton, partly a carry-over of intrauterine positioning, that remodels predictably toward valgus and then neutral as the child grows and begins to walk. Pathological varus arises when this remodelling is disturbed: in Blount disease abnormal compressive loading suppresses growth at the posteromedial proximal tibial physis, producing progressive tibia vara; in rickets defective mineralisation of the growth plate and metaphysis softens bone that then deforms under weight-bearing. Skeletal dysplasias, physeal injury, and focal growth disturbance are less common structural causes.
additionalDifferentials: Infantile or adolescent Blount disease (tibia vara)
Nutritional or hypophosphataemic rickets and other metabolic bone disease
Skeletal dysplasia such as metaphyseal chondrodysplasia or achondroplasia
Post-traumatic or post-infective physeal growth arrest
Focal fibrocartilaginous dysplasia of the proximal tibia
additionalInvestigations: Serial measurement of the intercondylar distance and clinical alignment
Standing full-length lower-limb radiographs with assessment of the metaphyseal-diaphyseal angle
Assessment of stature and growth against centile charts
Biochemical screen for rickets including calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and vitamin D metabolites where indicated
Renal and endocrine evaluation if a metabolic or renal cause is suspected
Skeletal survey or genetic assessment when a dysplasia is considered
redFlags: Progressive rather than improving deformity, or bowing persisting beyond the expected age
Short stature or disproportion suggesting a skeletal dysplasia or metabolic disease
Pain, a lateral thrust on walking, or an abrupt metaphyseal angulation suggesting Blount disease
Biochemical or dietary features pointing to rickets
reference.prognosis: Physiological bow legs resolve spontaneously with growth and carry an excellent prognosis, whereas pathological varus such as Blount disease or rickets can progress to fixed deformity and early joint degeneration if the underlying cause is not addressed.
pitfalls: Mistaking progressive Blount disease for benign physiological bowing and delaying treatment
Overlooking short stature or biochemical clues to rickets or a dysplasia
Failing to appreciate the normal varus-to-valgus developmental sequence and over-investigating a normal toddler
Not obtaining standing radiographs when the deformity is severe, asymmetrical, or painful
Assuming all bowing will resolve and omitting follow-up in atypical cases
management: Reassure and observe physiological genu varum, which corrects spontaneously with growth
Treat the underlying metabolic cause, replacing vitamin D and phosphate in rickets and addressing renal or endocrine disease
Trial bracing in early infantile Blount disease in the young child
Apply guided growth by lateral tension-band plating for progressive Blount disease or persistent pathological varus in the skeletally immature
Undertake realignment proximal tibial osteotomy for advanced Blount disease or fixed deformity
Monitor with serial intercondylar distance and standing radiographs assessing the metaphyseal-diaphyseal angle
Refer to paediatric orthopaedics when varus is asymmetrical, progressive, painful, or severe
